# Regulation, standards, and pricing power

This chapter answers two questions you raised directly: (1) are U.S. efficiency standards (SEER2) eroding under the Trump administration, and does it matter for a long-term investor; and (2) how much have the SEER2 and refrigerant changes actually raised equipment prices — the "average selling price (ASP) uplift" that can show up as a structural revenue tailwind.

## Are SEER2 standards eroding? Mostly no — but future tightening has stalled

The short version: **the 2023 SEER2 minimum-efficiency standards are still in force and have not been rolled back.** What the administration has done is freeze and challenge *new* and *future* rules, not repeal the existing floor. Three things are true as of mid-2026:

First, in February 2025 the DOE **postponed the implementation dates** of several Biden-era standards (touching central AC, water heaters, and other products) — a delay of *future* tightening, not a repeal of the 2023 baseline [^doe-postpone]. In May 2025, Congress used the Congressional Review Act to **permanently rescind** standards for *tankless gas water heaters, commercial refrigerators, and walk-in coolers* — real repeals, but **none of them residential AC/heat-pump SEER2 standards** [^cra]. Also in May 2025, DOE *proposed* a broad deregulatory package; it is proposed, contested, and faces near-certain litigation [^bd].

Second, there is a statutory backstop. The Energy Policy and Conservation Act contains an **"anti-backsliding" provision** that bars any new standard weaker than the one it replaces. This is why the existing SEER2 minimums are relatively safe; the practical effect of the current posture is that *future tightening is frozen*, not that today's floor falls [^doe-postpone].

Third, **ENERGY STAR survived.** After signals in 2025 that it might be eliminated, industry pushback kept it funded (~\$33M through FY2026) and moved it from EPA to DOE [^energystar]. Separately, federal *incentives* — notably heat-pump tax credits — are being wound down, which is a demand negative distinct from the standards themselves.

## Does the regulatory stall matter for a 10–15 year investor? Largely no

Even if U.S. federal tightening stays frozen, three forces sustain demand for efficient equipment over your horizon:

The biggest is **electricity prices**. The EIA projects U.S. average residential power around **18¢/kWh in 2026, up from ~17.3¢ in 2025**, and calls for the strongest multi-year electricity-demand growth since 2000 — driven heavily by data centers — with some regions (New England ~30¢, Pacific ~25¢) far above average [^eia]. Rising bills make efficiency a consumer economic decision regardless of any mandate. Second, **state standards and codes** (California and others) and the broader electrification trend persist independently: U.S. heat pumps already *outshipped* gas furnaces in 2025 [^heatpumps]. Third, **the EU is tightening, not loosening** — its revised F-Gas Regulation cuts HFC quotas hard and bans high-GWP refrigerants in new equipment on a faster schedule than the U.S., forcing the same manufacturers to keep investing in efficient, low-GWP designs [^fgas].

::: {.callout-note}
**Investor takeaway.** For a buy-and-hold horizon, treat the U.S. standards question as a second-order risk. The existing floor is protected by anti-backsliding; the durable demand drivers are rising electricity prices, state rules, EU regulation, and the economics of replacement — none of which depend on the federal administration tightening standards further. The clearer policy *negative* is the loss of U.S. heat-pump tax credits, which dampens near-term subsidy-driven demand.
:::

## The ASP uplift: how much did SEER2 + the refrigerant switch raise prices?

This is where regulation turns into a revenue tailwind. Two waves stacked:

**The 2023 SEER2 step** was widely reported to raise residential system prices by roughly **15–30%**, but those figures blended the efficiency mandate with general post-2020 inflation, so attribution is imprecise. Some technical commentators argue the true engineering cost of SEER2 compliance was only a few percent, implying much of the increase was pricing power rather than cost pass-through — a claim now echoed in litigation (below).

**The 2025 A2L refrigerant transition (R-410A → R-454B/R-32)** has the cleanest number. Analysts at William Blair, based on distributor checks in early 2025, estimated A2L would **raise HVAC equipment costs ~8–10%, and that the pricing was "sticking,"** with A2L products reaching ~90% of equipment sales by spring 2025 [^wb]. Lennox publicly announced a **~10% price increase** on its new R-454B residential products [^wb]. On top of that, tariffs added an estimated further few percent.

Whether the uplift *sticks* as a multi-year tailwind is the key question for Carrier, Trane, and Lennox. The evidence so far says yes: HVAC equipment producer prices have risen far faster than general goods prices since 2020, and manufacturers held list prices through the 2025 volume downturn rather than discounting.

::: {.callout-warning}
## A live overhang: antitrust litigation
The same pricing power that makes the ASP story attractive is now the subject of **antitrust class actions**. Beginning in early 2026, several price-fixing suits named Bosch, Carrier, Trane, Daikin, Lennox, Rheem, and AAON, alleging coordinated price increases and production cuts since 2020. **All defendants deny the allegations**, and the cases are unresolved — but this is a genuine, unquantified risk to the "ASP tailwind sticks" thesis and worth tracking [^antitrust].
:::

## Pre-buy / air-pocket: noise for your horizon

There was a clear 2024 pre-buy of R-410A equipment followed by a sharp 2025 destocking: combined AC + heat-pump shipments fell about **20% in 2025**, and Carrier's residential business fell ~40% in Q4 2025 as the channel worked off a multi-year inventory "overage" [^heatpumps]. For a 10–15 year investor this is a one-to-two-year inventory and transition distortion — it matters to 2025–2026 earnings optics and short-term traders, not to the long-run replacement-driven trajectory. I would only weight it heavily if it created a depressed entry valuation worth exploiting, or if the antitrust overhang above turned the "sticky pricing" into a liability.
